Taxi Boss Life

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Taxi Bosses. Powerful. Wealthy. Intimidating. We give you exclusive glimpse into a day in the life of a taxi boss.

Unique Selling Point:
- different perspective
- crime ridden industry
- true south african entrepreneurship - do or die.

Summary:
The taxi industry is shrouded with controversy. Taxi Drivers torment their fellow road users with their disregard of the rules of the road. It’s an industry estimated to be worth R50 billion annual with 69% of South African households using minibus taxis.

It’s a cut throat business, and if you don’t watch out you could get taken out.

Further information:
We all know taxi violence is rife. It’s brutal industry. It’s about money. And securing a route often means eliminating your competition.

KZN is notorious for taxi violence. Last year the Western Cape was in the spotlight with numerous shoot outs – at one stage, 13 drivers killed in just two weeks. In Gauteng, things are heating up. Just this weekend there was a hit on a taxi boss. 150 rounds were fired. He survived the hit, but is in hospital. We have footage of the shooting (from a distance, audio hectic, and you see them loading the injured taxi boss in the car)

They have heavy security and are under no illusion that they lead very controversial lives and securing transport routes is a deadly business.

These taxi bosses live in fear, they employ teams of body guards, the live sheltered lives because they know all too well they have targets on their backs. But we can’t forget that these guys are not innocent either, they too “protect” their routes.

Often South Africans bear the brunt of these taxi wars, but we never see what goes down from a taxi boss perspective. We spend a day in the life of taxi boss in the Western Cape.

We get to see the world through their eyes, the risks, the mitigation and ask if it’s worth it?

ADDITIONAL ELEMENTS
SECURITY COMPANY
We can interview a specialist security company focusing solely on providing protection for the taxi industry. It’s gotten so bad that the guards don’t drive in the same cars as the taxi bosses – they drive in front and behind – because the hitmen fire indiscriminately and these guards often get hit in a rain of bullets.

** We have cellphone footage of a recent hit in Bedfordview – 150 gun casings were picked up. It sounded like fireworks going off.

ROAD USERS HELD FOR RANSOM
We don’t want to glorify the Taxi Bosses either – so I think it is important to also include civilians that are being targeted by taxi associations. Regular South Africans that drop off staff along taxi routes are often stopped, keys taken away and then forced to pay up for daring to “steal” fees from the taxi bosses.

I have a great case study in that has had his staff transport stopped in Tembisa and held to ransom – he’s had to go and negotiate to get his vehicle released and has now been asked to cough up R400 a month for the privilege of giving his workers transport to and from work.

Script:


STRUCTURE: TAXI BOSS LIFE
VISUAL OPENING: TAXI CHAOS UPSOUNDS
Calling Commuters, getting in, putting money away…. HOOTING… TAXI’s BEHAVING badly, cutting
people off….driver shouting.
VO STARTS AT 00.05
VO: An industry laced with fear and loathing; apparently chaotic, unruly & largely unregulated.
It’s threatening, a law unto itself.
DRONE SHOT – SHOWING HOW THE TAXI MOVE IN PATTERN.
VO: But, take a step back from the noisy chaos, and something else emerges: a minibus taxi
industry that’s surprisingly organized – meticulously run, often with an iron fist.
VISUAL MOMENT – HERO SHOT INTRO
VO: This is Nkosekhaya Mnyanzeli - just 39, he owns 7 taxis and is the chairman of a long-
distance taxi association in Cape Town. He, is a taxi boss. Powerful, influential & Wealthy.
** AUDIO NOTE - TAXI DRIVE BY MOMENT - 1 seconds
LINK: Being a taxi boss means you call the shots, but that comes at a price. It's a cutthroat
business, and if you don't watch out, you'll get taken out.
BOSS: In this industry, things just happen and you don’t know why – you didn’t even know there
was an issue. I was sitting in the car, I heard the bullets hitting my body.
** AUDIO NOTE KEEP MAC WHISTLING
VO: It was at the Nyanga Taxi Rank back in 2015. Nine bullets fired at his car, hitting him in the
neck, left arm and the left side of his back - but it was not Nkosekhaya’s day to die.
BOSS: It’s dangerous, because if you have a high profile, you have more enemies because people
want your position. In the taxi industry there is money, but there is also death (pagad).
VO: We’re being given a rare glimpse into this secretive, often sinister world; an insight into a
day in the life of a taxi boss.
LINK: He's meeting with someone there from SANTACO but the guards are always there, heavily
armed in for quite a ride.
BOSS: We’re quickly going to the rank here and then from there to rank in Nyanga and finally to
Bellville.
VO5: There’s a seriousness about Nkosekhaya, he’s softly-spoken and reserved - not what you’d
expect from a tough Taxi Boss persona.
From humble beginnings as an Avanza driver in Umtata in 2001 he rose through the ranks,
becoming a taxi owner by 2016. Now, he’s a taxi association chairman - a respected position
among his peers.

2
BOSS: Everyone is scared to be a chairman, because if you are going to be a chairman you are going
to be killed. I told them that if they want me to be a chairman, I want guards. //
** AUDIO NOTE - CUT MAC Hhmmmm….hmmmmm….
VO: Nkosekhaya isn’t being dramatic. Just this week - there was an attempted hit outside the
office where we first met him. One of his guards was shot in the leg.
MAC: It’s dangerous, there are challenges – why do you still do it?
BOSS: I was raised here, I am able to make money here and I am able to raise my kids and I have a
house now through this business.
VO: It’s a bloody business shrouded in controversy - synonymous with violence 1 .
BOSS: When they don’t need you any more, they don’t ask you to step down, they just bring you
down with a gun. You come home with your child, they shoot you – wherever you are going, they
shoot you. When I leave my house, I have protection with me
VO: Here scores are often settled through the barrel of a gun… and not just in Cape Town.
Across the country, amateur video clips show just how ruthless this industry can be..
In Johannesburg, a taxi boss is shot in the head at point blank range…..
** AUDIO NOTE: LEAVE BREATHING MOMENT WHEN HE FALLS TO THE FLOOR
In the same city, a taxi boss is ambushed in a hail of bullets in a failed hit.
** AUDIO NOTE: LEAVE BREATHING MOMENT OF THE SHOTS BEING FIRED.
And in this clip from Gqeberha - a gunman crosses a busy road armed with a semi-automatic
rifle, letting rip in yet another taxi assassination.
** AUDIO NOTE: LEAVE BREATHING MOMENT…
In 2021, 123 taxi related murders were recorded. So far this year, there’ve been shootings
every single month 2 .
LINK: It's all about the money and securing your routes, which often means eliminating your
competition. And this applies even to regular road users.
VO: The industry transports close to 70% of South AFricans with an estimated 15 million
commuter trips every day - and none are spared its wrath when that market share is
threatened. Not even private companies transporting staff or the local school lift club.

1 SOME REPORTED TAXI KILLINGS IN LAST 12 MONTHS (15 dead, 7 injured)
DETAILED LIST IN NEXT FOOTNOTE
2 SOME REPORTED TAXI KILLINGS IN LAST 12 MONTHS (16 dead, 7 injured)
- AUGUST 2022 A taxi boss was killed in a drive-by shooting in Ingoqokazi, Inanda KZN – white Ford Ranger
- 27 JULY 2022 - PEDDIE, EC - attempted hit at the Border Alliance Taxi Association Rank
- 24 JUNE 2022 – TAXI BOSS KILLED PHOENIX
- 13 JUNE 2022 – TAXI BOSS DUNOON GUNNED DOWN
- JUNE 2022 - PMB TAXI DRIVER SHOT
- 15 JUNE 2022 – Taxi driver shot dead: Main Reef corner Beryll Street, Benoni. The taxi was loaded with children
- 19 MAY 2022 – Four Taxi Drivers – three people injured – FARADAY, JHB
- APRIL 2022 – CPT two taxi drivers who were shot and killed by unknown assailants in Bloekombos, Kraaifontein.
- MARCH 2022 – Two drivers gunned down – East London
- 27 MAY 2022 – BEDFORDVIEW SHOOTING – 3 shot and injured
- FEB 2022 – TAXI Driver shot in drive by Eastern Cape
- JAN 2022 – TAXI BOSS FOUND ON BEACH NEAR KHAYELITSHA
- 16 JULY 2021 - TAXI BOSS ASSASINATED IN GQEBERTHA EX- PORT ELIZABETH, EASTERN CAPE.

3
LEON: Basically taxi association, pulled the vehicle over, demanded that the vehicle is not allowed
to move.
VO: Leon Olivier owns a construction business in Johannesburg, his staff use a company truck to
get to and from work. But that’s not permitted by local taxi associations who often
confiscate the vehicle keys if not the entire car.
LEON: I need to go in. Come and negotiate fees with them.
MAC: But this doesn't seem fair. You know, I mean, obviously, it's illegal.
LEON: It's not acceptable. It affects everybody. If you live in your area, your mother, your sister,
your brother stays there and they all work in the same direction. So they're not allowed to
take transport with you. So you can't use your own vehicle. That's not on.
VO: The taxi bosses say it’s nothing personal, just business - protecting market share and profits.
BOSS: At 06.00 the taxis start operating, then we don’t want anyone taking staff at that time.
You’re taking from my income - what was meant for me.
VO: Business in a free market doesn’t work like that, but this is an industry that doesn’t like to
play by the rules. And not even the bosses themselves are immune.
Wherever he goes, Nkosekhaya is accompanied by a team of guards moving in convoy. As
we get closer to the rank – the mood in the car changes – the guard is on high alert.
BOSS: When I get to the rank, there is a place where people can take chances
MAC: I see that your protection gets out - why?
BOSS: Because they need to make sure that the place I am coming to is safe for me to get out //
UPSOUND BOSS: Molo! Molo! You’re alright? Everything good?
VO: This is where long distance bookings are made, cash is collected and paid over to the taxi
owners.
MAC: SO CHAIR, NoBODY’S tried to COME AND TAKE THE SAFE?
BOSS: NO, not at all.
Mac: Between me and you - So how much more or less?
BOSS: laughs
VO: The chairman is reluctant to put a figure to it - but confirms it’s a lot of cash.
To give you an idea, on average, a long distance taxi makes a monthly profit of around R37
000 , while on a short distance route, that figure is roughly R25000.
And with about 250 000 minibus taxis operating in South Africa 3 - it’s an industry easily
worth more than R50 billion 4 a year..

3 TAXI SA
4 https://businesstech.co.za/news/business/489691/heres-how-much-it-costs-to-own-and-run-a-taxi-in-south-
africa/

4
Of this, SARS reports that only R5 million is paid in company taxes - but Industry bodies 5 ,
insist they contribute billions to the country through VAT on car sales and fuel levies.
With much at stake, the industry has developed and enforces its own rules of engagement.
We stop off at a gathering of taxi bosses.
** AUDIO NOTE: UPSOUND MAC GREETING… Sanbonani Malunga - HELLO BOSSES
BOSS: Here is our office, this is where you plan the meetings and the way of working is planned
here. And the payments are being planned here and everything that needs to be done.
LINK: The bosses are about to have a meeting – so they’ve asked us please to step out so we can
give them a little bit of privacy.
VO: Taxi Associations are made up of taxi owners - the more taxi’s you have, the more say you
get. A Chairman wields significant power over the committee - he settles disputes and is
central to route allocations.
** AUDIO NOTE: Bring up ambient sounds
BOSS: Sometimes, there are some drivers that are drinking. Others go out with the taxi and don’t
sleep, because they have been drinking.
MAC: Do you have to be tough as a chairman.
BOSS: Yes, very tough.
VO: While rank managers take care of the day to day issues, taxi bosses still have to keep the
drivers in line.
** AUDIO NOTE: 1 second UPSOUND - hooting - bad driving behaviour.
VO: Because the same disregard for the rules of the road that makes ordinary motorists see red,
often hits taxi bosses in the pocket.
That’s clear at our next stop: a panel beater. Nkosekhaya needs to check on a recently
damaged taxi.
MAC: Mr. Andrew – how you?
MAC: it looks like it was a big accident – lots of damage
BOSS: Yes, it was damaged, but I told him to redo it completely and make it right, Because I don’t
want to put it on the road if it’s not in a good condition.
MAC: Safe for the people.
BOSS: Every passenger must feel safe in my taxi.
VO: And the safety of his family is also non-negotiable. Even collecting his children from school is
done with a convoy of armed guards.
8 year old Melisa is happy to see her dad.

https://www.businessinsider.co.za/what-you-need-about-the-state-of-sas-minibus-taxi-industry-including-
how-much-profit-owners-make-each-month-2020-1
5 TAXI SA

5

BOSS: Melisa, how was your day at school?
KIDS: Dad, it was good
LINK: So one of the most dangerous parts of being in this industry is leaving home or coming
home.
VO: His 13 year old son Vuyisani, is waiting for him at home.
BOSS: I don’t want them to be in the taxi industry at all. No. I always tell them that you are going to
be a doctor and you are going to be a lawyer. I wish they can be educated so that their lives
are not cut short.
VO: And yet, it’s a live and die by the sword reality that Nkosekhaya and others like him have
made their peace with. Often paying the ultimate, violent price.
ENDS

PROMOS
PROMO 1
VO: The taxi industry transports 69% of the country every single day – yet it’s an industry
shrouded with controversy.
BOSS: In the taxi industry there is money, but there is also death.
VO: We get a rare glimpse into the life of a taxi boss - as we ride along for the day with his
convoy of guards keeping watch.
PROMO 2 – 21 seconds
VO: The taxi industry rakes more than R50 billion every year. It’s a cut throat business – that
could cost you your life.
BOSS: When they don’t need you any more, they don’t ask you to step down, they just bring you
down with a gun.
VO: We get the inside track of the illusive taxi world through the eyes of a taxi boss.

PROMO 3 – 10 seconds
VO: They’re Influential, Wealthy and Intimidating. We give you an exclusive glimpse into the life
of a taxi boss and ask if it’s all worth it in this life and death business?

BOSS: At 06.00 the taxis start operating, then we don’t want anyone taking staff at that time. You’re taking from my income - what was meant for me. VO: Business in a free market doesn’t work like that, but this is an industry that doesn’t like to play by the rules. And not even the bosses themselves are immune. Wherever he goes, Nkosekhaya is accompanied by a team of guards moving in convoy. As we get closer to the rank – the mood in the car changes – the guard is on high alert. BOSS: When I get to the rank, there is a place where people can take chances MAC: I see that your protection gets out - why? BOSS: Because they need to make sure that the place I am coming to is safe for me to get out // UPSOUND BOSS: Molo! Molo! You’re alright? Everything good? VO: This is where long distance bookings are made, cash is collected and paid over to the taxi owners. MAC: SO CHAIR, NoBODY’S tried to COME AND TAKE THE SAFE? BOSS: NO, not at all. Mac: Between me and you - So how much more or less? BOSS: laughs VO: The chairman is reluctant to put a figure to it - but confirms it’s a lot of cash. To give you an idea, on average, a long distance taxi makes a monthly profit of around R37 000 , while on a short distance route, that figure is roughly R25000. And with about 250 000 minibus taxis operating in South Africa 3 - it’s an industry easily worth more than R50 billion 4 a year.. 3 TAXI SA 4 https://businesstech.co.za/news/business/489691/heres-how-much-it-costs-to-own-and-run-a-taxi-in-south- africa/ 4 Of this, SARS reports that only R5 million is paid in company taxes - but Industry bodies 5 , insist they contribute billions to the country through VAT on car sales and fuel levies. With much at stake, the industry has developed and enforces its own rules of engagement. We stop off at a gathering of taxi bosses. ** AUDIO NOTE: UPSOUND MAC GREETING… Sanbonani Malunga - HELLO BOSSES BOSS: Here is our office, this is where you plan the meetings and the way of working is planned here. And the payments are being planned here and everything that needs to be done. LINK: The bosses are about to have a meeting – so they’ve asked us please to step out so we can give them a little bit of privacy. VO: Taxi Associations are made up of taxi owners - the more taxi’s you have, the more say you get. A Chairman wields significant power over the committee - he settles disputes and is central to route allocations. ** AUDIO NOTE: Bring up ambient sounds BOSS: Sometimes, there are some drivers that are drinking. Others go out with the taxi and don’t sleep, because they have been drinking. MAC: Do you have to be tough as a chairman. BOSS: Yes, very tough. VO: While rank managers take care of the day to day issues, taxi bosses still have to keep the drivers in line. ** AUDIO NOTE: 1 second UPSOUND - hooting - bad driving behaviour. VO: Because the same disregard for the rules of the road that makes ordinary motorists see red, often hits taxi bosses in the pocket. That’s clear at our next stop: a panel beater. Nkosekhaya needs to check on a recently damaged taxi. MAC: Mr. Andrew – how you? MAC: it looks like it was a big accident – lots of damage BOSS: Yes, it was damaged, but I told him to redo it completely and make it right, Because I don’t want to put it on the road if it’s not in a good condition. MAC: Safe for the people. BOSS: Every passenger must feel safe in my taxi. VO: And the safety of his family is also non-negotiable. Even collecting his children from school is done with a convoy of armed guards. 8 year old Melisa is happy to see her dad. https://www.businessinsider.co.za/what-you-need-about-the-state-of-sas-minibus-taxi-industry-including- how-much-profit-owners-make-each-month-2020-1 5 TAXI SA 5 BOSS: Melisa, how was your day at school? KIDS: Dad, it was good LINK: So one of the most dangerous parts of being in this industry is leaving home or coming home. VO: His 13 year old son Vuyisani, is waiting for him at home. BOSS: I don’t want them to be in the taxi industry at all. No. I always tell them that you are going to be a doctor and you are going to be a lawyer. I wish they can be educated so that their lives are not cut short. VO: And yet, it’s a live and die by the sword reality that Nkosekhaya and others like him have made their peace with. Often paying the ultimate, violent price. ENDS PROMOS PROMO 1 VO: The taxi industry transports 69% of the country every single day – yet it’s an industry shrouded with controversy. BOSS: In the taxi industry there is money, but there is also death. VO: We get a rare glimpse into the life of a taxi boss - as we ride along for the day with his convoy of guards keeping watch. PROMO 2 – 21 seconds VO: The taxi industry rakes more than R50 billion every year. It’s a cut throat business – that could cost you your life. BOSS: When they don’t need you any more, they don’t ask you to step down, they just bring you down with a gun. VO: We get the inside track of the illusive taxi world through the eyes of a taxi boss. PROMO 3 – 10 seconds VO: They’re Influential, Wealthy and Intimidating. We give you an exclusive glimpse into the life of a taxi boss and ask if it’s all worth it in this life and death business?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Taxi Bosses. Powerful. Wealthy. Intimidating. We give you exclusive glimpse into a day in the life of a taxi boss.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: - different perspective - crime ridden industry - true south african entrepreneurship - do or die.
metadata.Summary: The taxi industry is shrouded with controversy. Taxi Drivers torment their fellow road users with their disregard of the rules of the road. It’s an industry estimated to be worth R50 billion annual with 69% of South African households using minibus taxis. It’s a cut throat business, and if you don’t watch out you could get taken out.
metadata.Further information: We all know taxi violence is rife. It’s brutal industry. It’s about money. And securing a route often means eliminating your competition. KZN is notorious for taxi violence. Last year the Western Cape was in the spotlight with numerous shoot outs – at one stage, 13 drivers killed in just two weeks. In Gauteng, things are heating up. Just this weekend there was a hit on a taxi boss. 150 rounds were fired. He survived the hit, but is in hospital. We have footage of the shooting (from a distance, audio hectic, and you see them loading the injured taxi boss in the car) They have heavy security and are under no illusion that they lead very controversial lives and securing transport routes is a deadly business. These taxi bosses live in fear, they employ teams of body guards, the live sheltered lives because they know all too well they have targets on their backs. But we can’t forget that these guys are not innocent either, they too “protect” their routes. Often South Africans bear the brunt of these taxi wars, but we never see what goes down from a taxi boss perspective. We spend a day in the life of taxi boss in the Western Cape. We get to see the world through their eyes, the risks, the mitigation and ask if it’s worth it? ADDITIONAL ELEMENTS SECURITY COMPANY We can interview a specialist security company focusing solely on providing protection for the taxi industry. It’s gotten so bad that the guards don’t drive in the same cars as the taxi bosses – they drive in front and behind – because the hitmen fire indiscriminately and these guards often get hit in a rain of bullets. ** We have cellphone footage of a recent hit in Bedfordview – 150 gun casings were picked up. It sounded like fireworks going off. ROAD USERS HELD FOR RANSOM We don’t want to glorify the Taxi Bosses either – so I think it is important to also include civilians that are being targeted by taxi associations. Regular South Africans that drop off staff along taxi routes are often stopped, keys taken away and then forced to pay up for daring to “steal” fees from the taxi bosses. I have a great case study in that has had his staff transport stopped in Tembisa and held to ransom – he’s had to go and negotiate to get his vehicle released and has now been asked to cough up R400 a month for the privilege of giving his workers transport to and from work.
